questions.prompt: Why did the Chinese and European scab methods carry more risk than Jenner's approach?

options.text: They used actual smallpox virus, which could cause the disease
They used toxoids that triggered dangerous allergic reactions
They used inactivated smallpox virus that couldn't protect
They used cowpox virus, which often caused severe cowpox

questions.prompt: Which vaccine type would be the safest choice for a severely immunocompromised patient, based on how the types work?

options.text: An attenuated whole-agent vaccine, since it reproduces a little
An inactivated or subunit vaccine, since nothing in it reproduces
Variolation, since the smallpox dose is carefully measured
Cowpox scabs, since cowpox is a mild disease in most people

questions.prompt: COVID monoclonal antibodies (Module 23) and COVID vaccines both target the spike protein. What's the key difference?

options.text: Both give passive immunity that fades after a few weeks
Vaccines contain antibodies; monoclonals contain spike mRNA
Monoclonals give passive immunity; vaccines build active immunity
Monoclonals use lipid nanoparticles; vaccines use hybridomas

questions.prompt: Which statement about antibiotic choice is FALSE?

options.text: Broad-spectrum drugs are always the better choice.
Broad-spectrum drugs suit unknown pathogens.
Killing normal flora can cause superinfections.
Narrow-spectrum drugs require a diagnosis.
Narrow-spectrum drugs spare more normal flora.

questions.explanation: Killing more bacteria isn't better — we want the bad guys only.

questions.prompt: Which explains why there are few antifungal and antihelminth drugs compared with antibacterials?

options.text: Fungi and worms have no metabolism for drugs to interfere with
Fungi and worms are viruses, so antibiotics can't reach them
Fungi and worms are not pathogens, so drugs aren't needed
Fungi and worms are eukaryotes like us, so selective toxicity is hard

questions.explanation: Slides: selective toxicity drops as the pathogen resembles the patient.

questions.prompt: Why do some antibiotics that target bacterial ribosomes have side effects (slides)?

options.text: They trigger variolation-like reactions in the patient
They block ACE2 receptors on the patient's own cells
They also target the peptidoglycan in human cell walls
Bacterial ribosomes resemble our mitochondrial ribosomes

questions.prompt: Antibiotic resistance is described as 'evolution on a short time scale.' Which scenario shows it?

options.text: Antibiotics directly make each bacterium stronger as it is exposed
Bacteria learn from the drug and teach other bacteria how to resist
The drug kills susceptible cells; the few resistant survivors multiply
Vaccines create resistant viruses that then infect the bacteria

questions.explanation: Natural selection, as in Module 18's warning to finish antibiotics.

options.text: Once the target bacteria are gone, the phages have no hosts left
Phages convert themselves into antibiotics after they attach
The immune system ignores phages until the bacteria are gone
Phages are programmed to kill themselves after one infection

why.C: The immune system doesn't ignore phages.

questions.prompt: Why would a lone pathogenic bacterium 'wait' to release toxins?

options.text: Its toxins only work in the dark, so it waits until nighttime to act
It can't make any toxins until it has divided at least a hundred times
Alone, its toxins would draw the immune system before it could overwhelm it
It needs the host's antibodies to bind it first before toxins can form

questions.prompt: Which pair of scientists' work is most directly connected by the idea of a targeted 'magic bullet'?

Jenner's cowpox vaccine and Pasteur's rabies vaccine
Fleming's penicillin and Bassler's quorum-sensing inhibitors
Chain's penicillin work and d'Hérelle's phage therapy

questions.explanation: Both deliver a toxic payload to a specific target.

questions.prompt: A clinic gives a broad-spectrum antibiotic before culture results return, then switches to a narrow-spectrum drug once the pathogen is identified. Why?

options.text: Narrow-spectrum drugs must always be given after broad ones
Start broad when the pathogen is unknown, then narrow to spare flora
Culture results make broad-spectrum drugs work more strongly
Broad drugs are cheaper, so they are only given for two days

questions.prompt: Which vaccine and Module 19 concept are linked?

options.text: Attenuated vaccines target the coagulase made by S. aureus
Toxoid vaccines target exotoxins like tetanus and diphtheria toxin
Subunit vaccines target the endotoxin (LPS) of Gram-negatives
mRNA vaccines target the siderophores that steal host iron

questions.explanation: Roux discovered diphtheria toxin; von Behring made antitoxin.

questions.prompt: Why does feeling sick after the second mRNA dose suggest the vaccine is working?

options.text: It means the first dose failed and the body is rejecting it
The vaccine contains live coronavirus that causes a mild case
The mRNA itself causes a short COVID infection in the cells
Cytokines from a strong immune response cause the symptoms

questions.explanation: The immune system is mounting an active response.

questions.prompt: Compare broad- and narrow-spectrum antibiotics: definition, example, when to use, and one risk.
questions.explanation: Broad-spectrum drugs act on many bacterial types (sulfanilamide, Cipro) and are used when the pathogen is unknown, but they kill normal flora, risking superinfection and resistance. Narrow-spectrum drugs act on few types (penicillin, vancomycin) and are used when the pathogen is known, sparing normal flora but requiring an accurate diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Trace the history of smallpox prevention from China to Jenner to Pasteur.
questions.explanation: Chinese (by early 1400s) inhaled smallpox scabs; Europeans (1700s) practiced variolation, placing smallpox scabs under the skin; Jenner used cowpox scabs (milkmaids rarely got smallpox) for a safer smallpox vaccine; Pasteur coined 'vaccine' (vacca = cow) and developed others, such as rabies.
